items.title: A 95% confidence interval does NOT mean there's a 95% chance the true value is in it
items.claim: Common claim: 'we are 95% confident the mean is between 4.2 and 5.7'. Often interpreted as 'there's a 95% probability the true mean is in this range'. In frequentist statistics this interpretation is technically wrong.
items.prompt: What does a 95% confidence interval actually mean?

options.text: The probability the parameter is in the interval is 95%

If you repeated the experiment many times and constructed a CI each time, 95% of those intervals would contain the true value. For a single interval, the true value is either in it or not — the 95% refers to the procedure's long-run reliability, not to a probability about the parameter
It's the same as a Bayesian credible interval

items.reveal:
In FREQUENTIST statistics, the true parameter (e.g., true mean mu) is treated as fixed, not random. The interval is random because it depends on the random sample. The interval either contains mu or it doesn't — probability 0 or 1.

The '95%' is a property of the PROCEDURE for generating the interval: across many hypothetical replications of the experiment, 95% of the intervals would contain the true mu. For your one observed interval, it either contains mu or doesn't.

In BAYESIAN statistics, the parameter is treated as random (described by a posterior distribution). A 95% credible interval IS the range where the parameter has 95% posterior probability of lying. The Bayesian interpretation is the one most people intuitively want.

Frequentist CIs and Bayesian credible intervals often look similar numerically — but they mean different things. The interpretation matters for inference and communication.

Why this distinction matters:
- Misinterpreting CIs leads to overconfidence in single results.
- Policy debates often hang on whether 'we are 95% sure' means anything actionable.
- Multiple comparisons (running many tests, picking 'significant' ones) inflate apparent CI coverage — see also: replication crisis.

Many statisticians (including Hoekstra et al. 2014) have shown that researchers across disciplines misinterpret CIs.

For most practical purposes, the Bayesian interpretation 'works'. But understanding the frequentist meaning matters for understanding what randomized inference does and doesn't guarantee.
items.why: Statistical results are commonly miscommunicated. Confidence intervals are a famous example: most users (including professionals) believe an interpretation the statistics don't support. Understanding the distinction is part of statistical literacy.

items.title: A 99% accurate medical test for a rare disease usually gives a false positive
items.claim: A test for a rare disease is 99% accurate (1% false positive rate, 1% false negative rate). The disease affects 1 in 10,000 people. You test positive. What's the chance you actually have the disease? Roughly 1%, not 99%.

options.text: Base rate matters. Out of 10,000 random people: ~1 truly has the disease (and tests positive); ~100 don't have it but test positive anyway (1% of 9999). Total positives ~101, true positives 1. So P(disease given positive) ≈ 1/101 ≈ 1%
False positives are impossible for accurate tests

items.reveal:
Bayes's theorem: P(disease | positive) = P(positive | disease) * P(disease) / P(positive).

P(positive | disease) = 0.99 (test sensitivity).
P(disease) = 0.0001 (base rate — the prevalence).
P(positive) = P(positive | disease) * P(disease) + P(positive | no disease) * P(no disease) = 0.99 * 0.0001 + 0.01 * 0.9999 ≈ 0.0001 + 0.01 = 0.0101.
P(disease | positive) = 0.99 * 0.0001 / 0.0101 ≈ 0.0098 = 0.98%.

The 'accuracy' of the test is misleading when the disease is rare. The vast majority of positives are FALSE positives, drawn from the much larger pool of healthy people.

Key insight: rare conditions produce rare true positives. Even excellent tests produce overwhelming numbers of false positives in screening contexts.

Real-world implications:
- Mass screening for rare cancers, HIV, etc., requires careful interpretation of positives.
- Drug tests at low real-prevalence give many false accusations.
- Airport security: very low base rate of terrorists; almost all positives are false alarms.
- Mammograms in the 40-49 age group: famous case of low base rate leading to controversy over screening recommendations.

Professionals routinely misinterpret. Gigerenzer's studies show many doctors get this wrong on similar problems. Communicating in 'natural frequencies' (1 in 10,000) rather than probabilities (0.0001) helps people reason correctly.
items.why: Test accuracy seems to translate directly to confidence in results. Bayes's theorem forces a different interpretation: when the condition is rare, even sensitive tests produce mostly false positives. Whole branches of medicine and public policy depend on getting this right.

items.title: If a stock falls 50% then rises 50%, you've LOST money
items.claim: Stock at 100. Falls 50%: now 50. Rises 50%: now 75. Two equal-percentage moves in opposite directions don't cancel.

options.text: Percentages are RATIOS, not amounts. The 50% drop reduces the base; the subsequent 50% rise is on a smaller base. To recover from a -50% loss you need a +100% gain

items.reveal:
To go from x to y, percentage change is (y - x) / x.

Loss of L percent: new value = old * (1 - L/100).
Gain of G percent: new value = old * (1 + G/100).

For symmetric percent moves NOT to cancel, multiply: (1 - 0.5)(1 + 0.5) = 0.75. Always less than 1 if the magnitude is the same.

Recovery table:
- Lose 10%: need 11.1% to recover.
- Lose 25%: need 33.3% to recover.
- Lose 50%: need 100% to recover.
- Lose 75%: need 300% to recover.
- Lose 90%: need 900% to recover.

Applications:
- Drawdowns in investing: deep losses require enormous gains to recover. A 50% bear market loss takes years of strong returns to break even.
- Discounted prices then surcharged: 50% off followed by 50% on actually leaves you at 75% of original price (consumer gets a deal).
- Inflation: 10% inflation for 7 years halves purchasing power, even though 70% < 100%.

Geometric vs arithmetic mean: a stock returning +50%, -50%, +50%, -50% has arithmetic mean return 0% but geometric (actual) mean of ((1.5 * 0.5 * 1.5 * 0.5)^0.25 - 1) = -13.4%/period.
items.why: Percentages feel symmetric. They're multiplicative ratios that don't cancel directly. Anyone interpreting investment returns, weight changes, price comparisons or compound growth without realising this misreads the data.
